newsitem.title: USA: Cohen opposes U.S. bill for early Bosnia pullout.
newsitem.headline: Cohen opposes U.S. bill for early Bosnia pullout.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen on Saturday repeated his opposition to a bill speeding withdrawal of U.S. troops from Bosnia, saying it would undercut NATO and harm Washington's ties with NATO allies.

A bill with bipartisan backing was introduced in the House on Thursday calling for withdrawal of all U.S. ground troops from Bosnia by the end of 1997, six months earlier than agreed under a NATO plan.

Cohen did not explicitly respond when asked if he would recommend that President Bill Clinton veto the measure, saying, "I would strongly oppose that particular measure. NATO has made an ... arrangement whereby we will keep our NATO forces in Bosnia until June of 1998."
Speaking on CNN's "Evans & Novak" programme, Cohen said legislating an earlier cutoff date was unnecessary and would harm NATO and strain Washington's relations with key allies.

"For us at this time to legislate a cutoff date prior to that time I think will undercut the NATO organisation as such," Cohen said. "It will cause some dissension. It will fracture relations to some degree. I think it's unnecessary."
He said U.S. troops were on track to leave by mid-1998, and if violence erupted in Bosnia, that would be the Bosnian government's concern, not Washington's.

The former senator from Maine said he realised Americans were sceptical about deployment of U.S. forces overseas, but felt they also recognised "that we made a major contribution to the peace in that region."

"We have seen a stopping of the killing, of the sniping, of the massacres that were accumulating. So we have made a very positive contribution," he said. "I think the American people would like to see an end to it, and we are preparing an end to that mission in June of 1998."
